collection_summary:
Original `qualitative` instance filling a gap-3 category. Existing Culture/Music subdomain — second Music-keyed instance after `notable_works_of_recent_nobel_literature_laureates`. NEW entity class: music genres × representative albums × artists — no other instance is keyed by music genre. Natural human query: 'For major music genres like Jazz, Rock, Hip hop, and Punk, what album is considered the genre's foundational or landmark work, and who recorded it?'

Multi-wiki source plan (20 URLs): 10 per-genre Wikipedia articles supply the universe + the article-foregrounded landmark album choice; 10 per-album Wikipedia articles supply Year of Release + Artist cross-validation. Genre articles define which album each genre treats as canonical (via lead-section emphasis or history-section structural prominence); per-album articles confirm release year and artist details.

Result: 10 rows × 4 columns (Genre PK + Landmark Album + Artist + Year of Release), single-key PK on Genre, 0 duplicates. Year range: 1959 (Kind of Blue, Jazz) to 2007 (Blackout, Pop) — spans nearly 50 years of recorded-music history. 10 distinct genres span Jazz, Country, Rock, Electronic, Heavy metal, Soul, Punk rock, Hip hop, Grunge, Pop. After cycle-2 audit-driven repair: Reggae dropped (Wikipedia article foregrounds Bob Marley as an artist but does not foreground any single Marley studio album in body text — Catch a Fire appears only in references); Grunge added (Wikipedia article's lead foregrounds Nirvana's Nevermind 1991 as the mainstream-breakthrough album); Soul's landmark Innervisions → Talking Book (precedence-of-mention tiebreaker for the co-equal Wonder trilogy in the Soul article).

Cycles 1+2+3 + Fields-Medal-cycles + painters-cycle + extinctions-cycles + deserts-cycles + tennis-cycles + this-instance-cycle-1+2 lessons applied upfront: (a) single PK on Genre (canonical Wikipedia article title for 9 of 10 genres; 'Hip hop music' is a disambiguating redirect-source to the broader 'Hip-hop' article — see normalization_decisions); (b) per-row data sourced from 2 articles each (genre + album); (c) explicit selection rule for Landmark Album ('most prominently described as foundational/era-defining/landmark in the genre's Wikipedia article, with the most narrative emphasis in lead/history-section position; ties broken by precedence of mention in article structure'); (d) curator-supplemented universe (10 of N possible major genres) with explicit exclusion rationale for Blues, Folk, Reggae, Funk, Disco, R&B documented in proposed_supplements; (e) audit-known-ambiguity flag for Pop music (the Pop article only weakly names Blackout — the album is mentioned as epitomizing a stylistic shift rather than as a genre-defining landmark); (f) similar partially_supplemented framing to the painters cycle (3 painters per movement per-article-cited).
source_coverage_notes:
Twenty Wikipedia source URLs combine. 10 per-genre articles define the universe + landmark-album choice; 10 per-album articles validate Year + Artist details for each chosen landmark.

Roles:
- source_urls[0] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz): universe + landmark-album selection. Foregrounds Kind of Blue (1959) — 'Miles Davis introduced the concept to the greater jazz world with Kind of Blue (1959), an exploration of the possibilities of modal jazz which would become the best selling jazz album of all time.' Strongest landmark signal in the staged set.
- source_urls[1] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music): universe + landmark-album. Foregrounds Modern Sounds in Country and Western Music (1962) — 'In 1962, Ray Charles topped charts with his country album Modern Sounds in Country and Western Music, creating country soul.' Other candidates (Wanted! The Outlaws 1976 — compilation excluded, Wide Open Spaces 1998, No Depression 1990) considered; Modern Sounds is the earliest studio album credited with creating a country sub-genre per the article.
- source_urls[2] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music): universe + landmark-album. Foregrounds Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band (1967) — '1967 saw the Beatles release their definitive psychedelic statement in Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band... Sgt. Pepper was later regarded as a starting point for the album era.' Rubber Soul and Revolver are also mentioned, but Sgt. Pepper has the strongest narrative emphasis.
- source_urls[3] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_music): universe + landmark-album. Foregrounds Switched-On Bach (1968) — 'The Moog synthesizer was brought to the mainstream in 1968 by Switched-On Bach... The album achieved critical and commercial success.' Trans-Europe Express (Kraftwerk, 1977) and Yellow Magic Orchestra (1978) are also cited; Switched-On Bach has the most narrative emphasis as the mainstream breakthrough.
- source_urls[4] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_metal_music): universe + landmark-album. Foregrounds Black Sabbath (1970) — 'Black Sabbath, which is generally accepted as the first heavy metal album.' Paranoid (also 1970) is co-equal in the article but Black Sabbath wins because of the explicit 'first heavy metal album' framing.
- source_urls[5] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_music): universe + landmark-album. Foregrounds Talking Book (1972, Stevie Wonder) — article cites 'progressive soul of the 1970s, Martin cites this period's albums from Wonder (Talking Book, Innervisions, Songs in the Key of Life)'. Three Wonder albums are co-equal in the article; under the precedence-of-mention tiebreaker, Talking Book is named first (cycle-2 audit fix: cycle-1 staged Innervisions as 'middle/most canonical' was an unsupported curator-judgment override of the declared tiebreaker rule).
- source_urls[6] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punk_rock): universe + landmark-album. Foregrounds Ramones (1976) — 'The Ramones are often described as the first true punk band, popularizing the punk movement in the United States... That April, the Ramones' debut album was released by Sire Records.' Stooges (1969) and The Clash (1977) are also cited; Ramones has the most narrative emphasis as 'first true punk band' debut.
- source_urls[7] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip_hop_music): universe + landmark-album. Foregrounds Raising Hell (1986, Run-DMC) — 'Run-DMC's third album, Raising Hell, was the first in the genre to be certified platinum on July 15, 1986.' Other 1987 landmarks (Criminal Minded, Yo! Bum Rush the Show, Paid in Full) and 1994 (Illmatic, Ready to Die) are mentioned; Raising Hell is the most singularly framed and earliest.
- source_urls[8] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grunge): universe + landmark-album. Foregrounds Nevermind (1991, Nirvana) — 'Grunge broke through into the mainstream in the early-to-mid-1990s, led by Nirvana's Nevermind in 1991, and followed by other crossover successes including Pearl Jam's Ten, Soundgarden's Badmotorfinger, and Alice in Chains' Dirt.' STRONG landmark signal — Nevermind is named in the lead as the genre-defining breakthrough (cycle-2 added Grunge as a replacement for the cycle-1 Reggae row).
- source_urls[9] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music): universe + landmark-album. Foregrounds Blackout (2007, Britney Spears) — 'This change was epitomized in Spears' highly influential 2007 album Blackout.' WEAK LANDMARK SIGNAL: Blackout is the only album mentioned by name in the entire Pop article, and only as a stylistic-shift epitomization rather than a genre-defining landmark. Audit may request Pop's removal; staged under the strict 'most prominently named album' rule because Blackout is the article's only named album.

- source_urls[15] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talking_Book): entity-detail for Talking Book, 1972, Stevie Wonder (cycle-2 swap replacing Innervisions for the Soul row).

Universe-size sanity: 10 staged rows = 10 curator-selected major music genres × 1 landmark album each. Genres excluded for lack of a clear single-studio-or-live-album landmark in their Wikipedia genre articles (full exclusion rationale in proposed_supplements): Blues, Folk (pre-LP-era field-recording traditions; articles cite only compilations); Reggae (article foregrounds Bob Marley as artist but no single Marley studio album in body text — Catch a Fire only in references); Funk (article foregrounds artists + singles like 'Cold Sweat', not LPs); Disco (article foregrounds the 1977 Saturday Night Fever soundtrack which is a multi-artist compilation, disqualified under the 'single studio or live album' rule); Rhythm and blues (singles-era genre; no LP foregrounded). 10 rows is exactly at the protocol's 10-row floor.
decision_log:
Candidate card (Stage 1 pre-gate, then Stage 2 scored axes per instance_selection_priorities.md):
- Pre-gate verdict: PASS with three documented risks resolved at staging. R1: 'landmark album' is curator-subjective unless source-grounded — committed to 'the album most prominently described as foundational/era-defining/landmark in the genre's Wikipedia article, with the most narrative emphasis; ties broken by precedence of mention in article structure'. R2: not every genre has a clear single-studio landmark in its Wikipedia article — committed to excluding genres without a clearly-named landmark studio album; cycle-1 dropped Blues + Folk, cycle-2 dropped Reggae and verified Funk/Disco/R&B exclusion (audit-driven research). R3: Pop music's Wikipedia article only weakly names Blackout — committed to including Pop with the weak-signal flag documented in open_questions.
- Seed/provenance: ORIGINAL. No example_questions.txt seed addresses music genres. Closest seed in shape is the `foundational_painters_of_major_modern_art_movements` instance (art movements × top-3 painters; partially_supplemented within-movement curator selection); this music-genre instance applies the same shape pattern but at 1-landmark-album-per-genre granularity.
- Category: qualitative (primary, the 'landmark album' selection is a qualitative judgment per-genre-article framing). Secondary: multi_attribute_projection (3 non-key attributes — Album, Artist, Year — exercise per-cell calibration).
- Source plan: 20 Wikipedia URLs (10 per-genre + 10 per-album). Genre articles define universe + landmark choice; album articles cross-validate Year + Artist.
- Expected shape: 10 rows × 4 cols, single PK on Genre.
- Domain: Culture/Music — existing subdomain in Culture family.
- Entity-class diversity (encouragement): music genres / albums / artists is a NEW entity class. Strong application of the entity-class-diversity encouragement.
- Risks/adaptation: per the three pre-gate risks above. Additional minor risks: (a) row count 10 at the protocol's 10-row floor; (b) qualitative judgments are genuinely subjective; (c) recency: Pop's Blackout (2007) is the most recent staged landmark.
- Decision: STAGE.

Further decisions:
1) Landmark Album selection rule: 'the album most prominently described as foundational, era-defining, or genre-defining in the genre's Wikipedia article, with the most narrative emphasis in lead-section or history-section position; ties broken by precedence of mention in article structure'. The album must be a single studio or live album (not a compilation, 'Greatest Hits', soundtrack with multiple artists, or singles collection).
2) Universe = 10 of N possible major music genres. Excluded genres (with audit-verified rationale documented in proposed_supplements): Blues, Folk (cycle-1; pre-LP-era field-recording traditions); Reggae (cycle-2 audit; no Marley studio album foregrounded in article body — Catch a Fire only in references); Funk (cycle-2 audit-verified; article foregrounds artists/singles not LPs); Disco (cycle-2 audit-verified; Saturday Night Fever soundtrack is multi-artist compilation); Rhythm and blues (cycle-2 audit-verified; singles-era genre).
3) Pop music inclusion despite weak signal: the Pop article only names one album (Blackout 2007) and only as a 'stylistic-shift epitomization'. Pop is staged because (a) it is unambiguously a major music genre, (b) the article does name an album per the strict rule, (c) the weak signal is explicitly flagged in open_questions. An audit could request Pop's removal — cycle-3 fallback option.
4) Ties-within-article (precedence-of-mention tiebreaker, per the declared rule): the staged choice prefers (a) explicit 'first' or 'foundational' framing if present (Black Sabbath, Raising Hell, Ramones), else (b) precedence of mention in article structure (Talking Book first-named of the Wonder trilogy in Soul article — cycle-2 audit corrected the cycle-1 Innervisions 'middle of cluster' override), else (c) earliest-in-time studio release (Modern Sounds for Country's multi-candidate cluster).
5) Genre name normalization: disambiguating common-form names — 'Jazz', 'Country music', 'Rock music', 'Electronic music', 'Heavy metal music', 'Soul music', 'Punk rock', 'Hip hop music', 'Grunge', 'Pop music'. For most genres the staged form is the canonical Wikipedia article title. The 'music' suffix is present where Wikipedia disambiguates the genre from a broader concept (Rock music vs Rock, Pop music vs Pop, Heavy metal music vs heavy metal chemistry, Soul music vs the concept of soul). 'Jazz', 'Grunge', 'Punk rock' stand without 'music' suffix per their canonical Wikipedia article titles. For 'Hip hop music': the canonical Wikipedia article title is 'Hip-hop' (the article covers both the music genre and the broader culture); 'Hip hop music' is a redirect into 'Hip-hop' — the staged form follows the redirect-source convention because the schema is explicitly about the music genre, not the broader culture. Cycle-2 audit fix: cycle-1 incorrectly said 'Heavy metal (no music suffix per article title)' — the article title is actually 'Heavy metal music'. Cycle-4 audit fix: clarified that 'Hip hop music' is the disambiguating redirect-source rather than the canonical article title.
6) Album name normalization: full Wikipedia article-title form, WITHOUT parenthetical disambiguation where the album title is unambiguous in display: 'Ramones (album)' Wikipedia URL but staged 'Ramones'; 'Black Sabbath (album)' URL but staged 'Black Sabbath'; 'Blackout (Britney Spears album)' URL but staged 'Blackout'.
7) Artist name normalization: Wikipedia article-title form. Bands as singular entities ('The Beatles', 'Ramones', 'Black Sabbath', 'Nirvana', 'Run-DMC').
8) Year of Release: numeric integer; the year the album was first released. For albums with multiple regional release dates, the earliest is used.
9) Sort order: Year of Release ASC primary (chronological), Genre ASC secondary tiebreaker.
10) operation_type 'join' chosen — genre ⋈ album via the landmark-album relation. No multi-row aggregation per genre (1-album-per-genre rule).
11) claim_type 'partially_supplemented' — universe of 10 genres is a curator subset of N possible major genres (Blues, Folk, Reggae, Funk, Disco, R&B excluded per source-faithfulness rule); landmark-album choice within each genre is grounded in the article via the explicit selection rule + precedence-of-mention tiebreaker. Both layers of curator-supplementation documented in proposed_supplements.
normalization_decisions: Genre (PK) values use disambiguating common-form names that map to a single Wikipedia article each: 'Jazz', 'Country music', 'Rock music', 'Electronic music', 'Heavy metal music', 'Soul music', 'Punk rock', 'Hip hop music', 'Grunge', 'Pop music'. For most genres the staged form is the canonical Wikipedia article title (Heavy metal music, Country music, Rock music, Electronic music, Soul music, Pop music, Jazz, Grunge, Punk rock). For 'Hip hop music', the canonical Wikipedia article title is actually 'Hip-hop' (covering both the music genre and the broader culture); 'Hip hop music' is a redirect that disambiguates to the music-genre framing — the staged form follows the redirect-source convention because the schema is explicitly about music genres, not the broader culture. Cycle-2 audit fix: cycle-1 had inconsistent normalization claiming 'Heavy metal (no music suffix per article title)' which was incorrect — the article title is 'Heavy metal music'. Cycle-4 audit fix: tightened the narrative to acknowledge that 'Hip hop music' is the disambiguating redirect-source rather than the canonical article title. Landmark Album values use Wikipedia article-title form WITHOUT parenthetical disambiguation: 'Kind of Blue', 'Modern Sounds in Country and Western Music', 'Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band', 'Switched-On Bach', 'Black Sabbath', 'Talking Book', 'Ramones', 'Raising Hell', 'Nevermind', 'Blackout'. Artist values use Wikipedia article-title form, treating bands as singular entities ('The Beatles', 'Black Sabbath', 'Ramones', 'Nirvana', 'Run-DMC'). Year of Release is numeric integer, taking the album's first-release year per its Wikipedia article infobox. Sort order: Year of Release ASC primary, Genre ASC secondary tiebreaker.
open_questions: 1) Universe selection: 10 of N major music genres are staged. Excluded genres (Blues, Folk, Reggae, Funk, Disco, R&B) all lack a clear single-studio-or-live-album landmark in their Wikipedia articles (full rationale in proposed_supplements). An audit could request expansion by relaxing the 'single studio album' rule to allow compilations (enabling Blues with Robert Johnson 'King of the Delta Blues Singers' 1961 compilation, Folk with Anthology of American Folk Music 1952). 2) Pop music's weak landmark signal: the Pop article only names 'Blackout' (Britney Spears, 2007) and only as a stylistic-shift epitomization. The Pop genre is more singles-driven than album-driven per the article's own framing. An LLM under test might reasonably name 'Thriller' (Michael Jackson, 1982) or other widely-cited pop albums even though the Pop genre article doesn't foreground them. 3) Soul music tie-breaker applied (cycle-2 audit fix): the Soul article cites Talking Book / Innervisions / Songs in the Key of Life as co-equal Stevie Wonder albums; under the precedence-of-mention tiebreaker, Talking Book (first-named) wins. An LLM naming Innervisions or Songs in the Key of Life could be partially credited. 4) Heavy metal tie: Black Sabbath / Paranoid (both 1970, both Sabbath) are co-equally cited. Staged Black Sabbath because the article explicitly says it 'is generally accepted as the first heavy metal album'. An LLM naming Paranoid could be partially credited. 5) Grunge landmark: Nevermind (1991, Nirvana) is unambiguously foregrounded as the genre's mainstream-breakthrough album. Alternative-rock article also foregrounds Nevermind — would collide if Alternative rock were added, so Alternative rock is excluded from this instance. 6) Hip hop landmark: Raising Hell (1986) is the chosen first-platinum-album landmark; other strong candidates include Public Enemy 'It Takes a Nation of Millions' (1988), N.W.A 'Straight Outta Compton' (1988), Dr. Dre 'The Chronic' (1992), Nas 'Illmatic' (1994), or The Notorious B.I.G. 'Ready to Die' (1994). An LLM naming any of these could be partially credited. 7) Country music tie: Modern Sounds in Country and Western Music (1962) is the earliest sub-genre-creator candidate; an LLM naming Red Headed Stranger (Willie Nelson, 1975), At Folsom Prison (Johnny Cash, 1968), or Wanted! The Outlaws (1976, compilation — flagged) could be partially credited. 8) Genre-name suffix inconsistency: 'Jazz', 'Grunge', 'Punk rock' stand without 'music' suffix per their canonical Wikipedia article titles. 'Country music', 'Rock music', 'Electronic music', 'Heavy metal music', 'Soul music', 'Pop music' have the 'music' suffix per their canonical Wikipedia article titles (Wikipedia disambiguates the genre from a broader concept). 'Hip hop music' is intentionally NOT canonical — Wikipedia's canonical article title is 'Hip-hop' (covering both the music genre and the broader culture); 'Hip hop music' is a redirect into that article, chosen for the staged form because the schema is explicitly about the music genre, not the broader culture. An LLM normalizing to a uniform form (e.g., all-with-suffix or all-without) is responding to the across-genres inconsistency, not the schema's intent. An LLM responding with 'Hip-hop' (canonical Wikipedia title) instead of 'Hip hop music' (staged redirect-source) is defensible under canonical-title reading. 9) Album-title parenthetical disambiguation: staged Landmark Album values strip the parenthetical (Wikipedia URL 'Ramones_(album)' but staged 'Ramones'; 'Blackout_(Britney_Spears_album)' but staged 'Blackout'); an LLM responding with the full disambiguated form is honoring the URL form rather than the display form. 10) Year of Release for re-released albums: each staged year is the album's first-release year per its Wikipedia infobox.
proposed_supplements:
The 10-row staged universe is a curator-supplemented subset of the N possible major music genres covered by Wikipedia. Two layers of curator-supplementation are documented:

(1) Genre-universe supplementation (which genres are in vs out): 10 genres are included (Jazz, Country, Rock, Electronic, Heavy metal, Soul, Punk rock, Hip hop, Grunge, Pop). 6 genres were considered but excluded after cycle-1 + cycle-2 audit-verified research, each with a specific source-faithfulness reason:
- Blues (cycle-1) — Wikipedia 'Blues' article treats blues as a pre-LP-era folk tradition and does not foreground any single studio album as landmark. The few albums named (Endless Boogie 1971, Strong Persuader 1986, Texas Flood 1983, Alabama Blues) appear only as career markers for individual artists, not as genre-defining works.
- Folk (cycle-1) — Wikipedia 'Folk music' article centers on field-recording traditions; the only anthology cited (Anthology of American Folk Music, Harry Smith, 1952) is a multi-artist compilation, disqualified under the 'single studio or live album' rule.
- Reggae (cycle-2 audit-driven) — Wikipedia 'Reggae' article foregrounds Bob Marley as an artist (17 mentions) but does not foreground any single Marley studio album in body text. Catch a Fire appears only in references; The Harder They Come (1972) is a multi-artist soundtrack disqualified under the rule. Replaced by Grunge in cycle-2.
- Funk (cycle-2 audit-verified) — Wikipedia 'Funk' article foregrounds artists (James Brown, Parliament-Funkadelic, Sly and the Family Stone) and singles ('Cold Sweat', 'Maggot Brain' title track) rather than LPs. No single studio album is foregrounded.
- Disco (cycle-2 audit-verified) — Wikipedia 'Disco' article foregrounds the 1977 Saturday Night Fever soundtrack as the genre's breakthrough, but this is a multi-artist compilation, disqualified under the 'single studio or live album' rule. No qualifying single-studio fallback is foregrounded.
- Rhythm and blues (cycle-2 audit-verified) — Wikipedia 'Rhythm and blues' article structures around artists, labels, and singles (Louis Jordan, Big Joe Turner, Fats Domino), not LPs. Classic R&B is a 78-rpm singles-era genre, predating the LP-as-statement format; no album is foregrounded.

(2) Within-genre landmark-album supplementation (which album per genre): the selection rule ('most prominently described as foundational/landmark; ties broken by precedence of mention in article structure') is fully article-grounded for the strong-signal genres (Jazz, Rock, Heavy metal, Punk rock, Hip hop, Grunge — 6 of 10 rows). For genres where the article cites multiple co-equal candidates, the tiebreaker is applied:
- Soul music: precedence-of-mention picks Talking Book (first-named of the Wonder trilogy in the article).
- Heavy metal: explicit 'first heavy metal album' framing picks Black Sabbath over Paranoid.
- Country music: earliest sub-genre-creator framing picks Modern Sounds over later candidates.
- Electronic music: 'mainstream breakthrough' framing picks Switched-On Bach over Kraftwerk/YMO.
- Pop music: only one album is named in the article (Blackout) — the staged choice follows the strict rule even though the framing is weak; flagged in open_questions as audit-known-ambiguity. An audit could request Pop's removal in cycle-3, reducing the universe to 9 rows (sub-floor under the 10-row protocol) — and so the suggested expansion path is to add 1-2 more genres with clear landmarks rather than drop Pop. Cycle-2 audit-verified candidates that did NOT meet the rule (Funk, Disco, R&B, Alternative rock — collides with Grunge on Nevermind, Bossa nova, Salsa) constrain expansion options; future cycles may relax the 'single studio or live album' rule for pre-LP-era genres to enable Blues/Folk inclusion via compilations.

cycle_1.summary: Cycle-1 was the audit pass on the initial-stage artifact. Auditor flagged 3 BLOCKING (missing proposed_supplements; Reggae not source-supported; Soul tie-breaker rule violated) + 2 hygiene (Heavy metal/Hip hop normalization prose; Folk/Anthology over-specific rationale) + 1 suggestion (expand universe to 12-14 rows). See cycle_2 for repair details.

cycle_2.verdict: Repair pass — addressing cycle-1 audit findings
blocking_addressed: B1 (structural, BLOCKING — missing proposed_supplements field): cycle-1 declared claim_type 'partially_supplemented' but did not include a proposed_supplements field documenting the curator-supplementation audit trail. Cycle-2 fix: added the proposed_supplements field at the top level of curation.json with full two-layer documentation: (1) genre-universe supplementation (10 of N genres included; 6 excluded with per-genre source-faithfulness reasoning for Blues, Folk, Reggae, Funk, Disco, R&B); (2) within-genre landmark-album supplementation (selection rule + precedence-of-mention tiebreaker, plus the Pop weak-signal exception).

B2 (scope, BLOCKING — Reggae not source-supported): cycle-1 staged Reggae → Catch a Fire (1973, Bob Marley and the Wailers), but the Wikipedia Reggae article does not foreground this album in body text — Catch a Fire appears only in references. Cycle-2 fix: dropped the Reggae row entirely. To compensate for the row loss (would drop from 10 to 9 rows, below the protocol floor), added Grunge → Nevermind (1991, Nirvana) as a replacement — the Wikipedia Grunge article's lead explicitly names Nevermind as the mainstream-breakthrough album ('Grunge broke through into the mainstream in the early-to-mid-1990s, led by Nirvana's Nevermind in 1991'). source_urls updated: removed https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggae and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catch_a_Fire; added https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grunge and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevermind. CSV row Reggae removed; Grunge added with sort placement between Hip hop 1986 and Pop 2007. Cycle-2 audit-driven research also verified that 4 other expansion candidates (Funk, Disco, R&B, Alternative rock) have NO viable single-studio landmark in their Wikipedia articles, so the universe remains at 10 rows.

B3 (structural, BLOCKING — Soul tie-breaker rule violation): cycle-1 staged Soul → Innervisions (1973, Stevie Wonder) and justified it as 'middle/most canonical' of the Wonder trilogy. The Soul article actually cites the three albums in order Talking Book / Innervisions / Songs in the Key of Life — under the declared precedence-of-mention tiebreaker, Talking Book (1972, first-named) wins. The cycle-1 'middle/most canonical' justification was an unsupported curator-judgment override of the declared rule. Cycle-2 fix: CSV row changed Soul → Innervisions (1973) to Soul → Talking Book (1972); source_urls updated: removed https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Innervisions, added https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talking_Book; sort placement shifts Soul from 1973 to 1972 (now between Heavy metal 1970 and Punk rock 1976).
hygiene_addressed: H1 (structural, HYGIENE — Heavy metal / Hip hop normalization prose inaccurate): cycle-1 decision_log Rule 5 said 'Heavy metal (no music suffix per article title)' but the actual Wikipedia article title is 'Heavy metal music'. Cycle-2 fix: (a) corrected CSV Genre value 'Heavy metal' → 'Heavy metal music' to match the article title; (b) rewrote decision_log Rule 5 + normalization_decisions to consistently describe the 'music' suffix convention (Hip hop music, Heavy metal music, Rock music, Pop music, Soul music, Electronic music, Country music all have suffix per Wikipedia disambiguation; Jazz, Grunge, Punk rock do not). The cycle-1 narrative was internally inconsistent for both Heavy metal and Hip hop music.

H2 (scope, HYGIENE — Folk/Anthology rationale over-specific): cycle-1 source_coverage_notes said 'Folk centers on field-recording archives (Alan Lomax — 18 mentions)' which gave overly granular detail (the 18-mentions count). Cycle-2 fix: tightened the Folk exclusion rationale in proposed_supplements to 'field-recording traditions; only compilation cited is multi-artist, disqualified under the rule' — removed the granular Lomax-mention-count detail.
suggestion_addressed: S1 (scope, SUGGESTION — expand universe to 12-14 rows): cycle-1 audit suggested expansion via Funk / Alternative rock / Grunge / Disco / Bluegrass / Gospel / R&B / Bossa nova / Salsa. Cycle-2 audit-driven research (per the cycle-1 audit suggestion) evaluated Funk + Alternative rock + Grunge + Disco + R&B and found: only Grunge has a STRONG landmark signal (Nevermind in the Grunge article's lead); Alternative rock collides with Grunge on Nevermind (same album foregrounded); Disco's Saturday Night Fever is a disqualifying multi-artist soundtrack; Funk and R&B have NO single-studio landmark foregrounded. Net: Grunge added as the replacement for Reggae (1 row swap, not an expansion). Universe remains at 10 rows. The cycle-1 suggestion to expand to 12-14 rows could not be honored under the strict 'single studio or live album' rule; relaxing the rule for pre-LP-era genres (Blues, Folk, R&B) is a possible cycle-3 expansion path documented in proposed_supplements.

cycle_3.summary: Cycle-3 was the re-audit pass on the cycle-2-repaired artifact. Auditor verified all 3 cycle-1 BLOCKING + 2 HYG + 1 SUGGESTION fixes landed (proposed_supplements substantive, Reggae→Grunge swap correct, Soul→Talking Book correct, Heavy metal music normalized, source_urls updated to 20), and the Ready verdict was issued. 2 non-blocking hygiene findings carried forward to cycle_4: (a) Hip_hop_music redirects to Wikipedia's Hip-hop article, so the 'exact article-title form' normalization prose still overclaims; (b) draft._extraction_notes still carried older Blues/Folk-only exclusion prose and should be refreshed to the cycle-2 Reggae/Grunge/Funk/Disco/R&B state.

cycle_4.verdict: Ready — hygiene cleanup pass after Ready verdict
hygiene_addressed: H1 (structural, HYGIENE — Hip-hop redirect prose overclaims canonical-title status): cycle-3 audit flagged that the staged 'Hip hop music' Genre value is not the canonical Wikipedia article title — the canonical article is 'Hip-hop' (covering both the music genre and broader hip-hop culture); 'Hip hop music' is a redirect into it. The cycle-2 normalization prose claimed all 10 Genre values were 'canonical Wikipedia article titles', which was true for 9 of 10 but inaccurate for Hip hop music. Cycle-4 fix: rewrote normalization_decisions + decision_log Rule 5 to acknowledge that 'Hip hop music' is the disambiguating redirect-source rather than the canonical article title; the staged form is preferred because the schema is explicitly about the music genre, not the broader culture (which the 'Hip-hop' canonical article also covers). No CSV change — the redirect-source form is semantically correct for a music-genre-focused schema.

H2 (scope, HYGIENE — draft._extraction_notes still carried older Blues/Folk-only exclusion prose): cycle-2 updated collection_summary + source_coverage_notes + proposed_supplements to reflect the expanded exclusion list (Blues, Folk, Reggae, Funk, Disco, R&B) but draft._extraction_notes still said only 'Blues + Folk excluded at cycle-1'. Cycle-4 fix: rewrote draft._extraction_notes to reflect the full cycle-2 exclusion state (6 genres excluded after cycle-1 + cycle-2 audit-verified research); the lessons-applied (d) bullet now points to proposed_supplements for the per-genre rationale rather than naming Blues/Folk alone.

cycle_5.verdict: Ready — hygiene propagation pass after audit-cycle-3 Ready verdict (1 HYG)
hygiene_addressed: H1 (structural, HYGIENE — redirect framing not fully propagated): audit cycle 3 verified that normalization_decisions + decision_log Rule 5 + draft._extraction_notes exclusion list were correctly updated in cycle-4, but flagged that the blanket 'Wikipedia article-title form' wording still appeared in three other active locations: collection_summary lessons-applied bullet (a), draft._extraction_notes lessons-applied bullet (a), and open_questions item 8 ('others have music suffix per their disambiguating Wikipedia titles' implicitly treats all 10 genres as canonical-title forms). Cycle-5 fix: narrowed all three locations to acknowledge that 9 of 10 genres are canonical Wikipedia article titles while 'Hip hop music' is a disambiguating redirect-source. collection_summary bullet (a) now says 'canonical Wikipedia article title for 9 of 10 genres; Hip hop music is a disambiguating redirect-source to the broader Hip-hop article'. draft._extraction_notes bullet (a) gets the same treatment. open_questions item 8 now explicitly notes that 'Hip hop music' is intentionally NOT canonical (Wikipedia's canonical is 'Hip-hop'), staged as a redirect-source to focus on the music genre rather than the broader culture; an LLM answering 'Hip-hop' instead of 'Hip hop music' is defensible under canonical-title reading.
